content: Center for Food Safety, the Center for Biological Diversity, and Pesticide Action & Agroecology Network North America have sued the Trump administration over the registration of trifludimoxazin, a potent PFAS pesticide that breaks down into long-lived, PFAS byproducts. PFAS, or perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are a class of chemicals characterized by ultra-strong carbon-fluorine bonds that are highly resistant to break down. Trifludimoxazin takes years to decades to break down. The groups’ lawsuit was filed Friday in the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. The Environmental Protection Agency has approved the use of trifludimoxazin on many crops, including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, oranges, apples, peanuts and almonds, despite acknowledging the chemical’s potential harms to wildlife and human health. “Trifludimoxazin is a likely human carcinogen that belongs to a family of weedkillers that also causes reproductive harm, birth defects and neurological deficits in animal studies,” said Bill Freese, science director at Center for Food Safety. “As if the health threats weren’t enough, this incredibly potent herbicide can drift to stunt crops and wild plants hundreds of yards from a sprayed field, while runoff threatens wetland plants. Potent biocides like this have no business on the American landscape.” The EPA acknowledges that trifludimoxazin causes thyroid tumors in rodent studies but did not assess the cancer risk to farmworkers who use the pesticide or to people exposed to trifludimoxazin-contaminated food or water. Spray drift is likely to result in widespread harm to native plants and crops grown for food. Trifludimoxazin is 10 times more toxic to plants than dicamba, the herbicide whose rampant drift and runoff has caused unprecedented damage across many millions of acres of crops since 2017. “While everyone’s distracted by the Trump administration’s erratic actions on the world stage, it keeps approving dangerous forever pesticides right here on our own soil,” said Nathan Donley, environmental health science director at the Center for Biological Diversity. “It’s unconscionable, immoral and illegal. Our kids and grandkids deserve better than to be saddled with pollution that never goes away.” “Continuing to register new herbicides like trifludimoxazin keeps farmers on the pesticide treadmill and perpetuates the problem of herbicide resistance in weeds,” said Emily Marquez, Ph.D, staff scientist with Petitioner Pesticide Action & Agroecology Network North America. “The potential for PFAS pesticides to contaminate water and soil wherever they are used is highly concerning for the health and livelihoods of people in farming communities.” Trifludimoxazin is one of many currently registered herbicides that kill plants by shutting down an enzyme (protoporpyhyrinogen oxidase, or PPO) that is also present in people. content: A strange thing happened to me in a deserted parking lot on a recent Sunday morning: My 16-year-old daughter actually asked me a question. I was telling her everything I know about reversing a car without the help of a backup camera. “First turn your whole body, shoulders rotated, right hand on the back of the passenger seat, until you’re looking out the rear window at the world behind you.” Her hands were on the wheel. Her phone was face down in the cup holder. She turned her body the way I’d suggested and nudged the wheel to the left, and the car floated backward in a woozy arc that wasn’t quite what she’d intended. “Wait,” she said. “Do I turn with both hands? Did I do that wrong?” I want to stop here, because I don’t think I can convey just how unusual such an exchange is these days—her listening to me and asking for help. Sometime in the past year, she stopped wanting anything from me other than my credit card and maybe my nicest suede boots. She definitely stopped wanting my instruction, my opinion, my take on anything, having concluded that she already understands pretty much everything. The talking is what I have missed. For 14 or 15 years, my daughter narrated in a fire hose of chatter—to me, to her father, to whoever. So much talking: about why the sun sets, the kid she was mad at, the plot of a show she was three episodes into, how she wanted to decorate her room. Around the start of high school, the talking thinned out, siphoned almost exclusively to her friends. Nothing announced the change. It went the way a baby tooth goes, loose for a while and then simply absent. [ Helen Lewis: I’m the driver now ] When she got a learner’s permit, some measure of talking reappeared. It wasn’t fully restored, exactly, but confined within one small, sealed space that moves. Inside the car, she knows she doesn’t know: In no version of parallel parking can she wing it without asking for tips from someone who has done it 10,000 times. Learning to drive is something she cannot fake her way through. This wobbly uncertainty, this return to a kind of innocence, is the rarest condition in a 16-year-old, and it lasts about as long as a learner’s permit does. So my daughter asks, and listens, and we manage to simply talk in some of the ways we haven’t in a long time: about what her friends did over the summer, which kid at the pool where she lifeguards asked her if she could babysit them. For an hour at a stretch I get a version of my daughter that I had filed away as gone for good. But this is also, in some ways, the worst hour of my week, because the terms of a driving lesson are the exact inverse of the many other kinds of lessons that came before it. Everything else I ever taught my daughter, I did with one hand on the thing: I steadied the tail end of the bike, I held the knife and moved her fingers back from the blade, I grasped her hand crossing Seventh Avenue for so many years that my palm still expects to find hers at intersections. content: No matter how you read it, The Power Broker is a serious undertaking. The paperback weighs as much as a brick; to avoid lugging around all 1,344 pages, people have cut it apart at the spine and chunked it into sections. Others have organized in-person Power Broker marathon readings that run continuously for three full days. I decided to try something else. Over the past several weeks, I’ve spent 10 hours paging through Robert Caro’s masterpiece on an e-reader the size of a credit card. It’s magnetic, and small enough to attach to the back of my iPhone without adding any real bulk to my pocket. (Yes, this does mean that I have a screen on the back of another screen.) It’s called the Xteink X3, and at a glance, it looks like a cheap gimmick: more electronic junk made by unknown brands and sold on Temu and TikTok Shop—the kind of thing influencers are always hawking. (Can I interest you in a programmable LED hat for $11.60? Or how about $20 AirPod look-alikes made by “Fhumsh”?) In a sense, it is that. Xteink sounds less like a real brand name than the kind of garbled text you’ll find in AI-slop memes. (Speaking of which, the official website of the China-based company is full of AI-generated photos of people posing with the device.) And indeed, since the X3’s release on Amazon in May, TikTokers and YouTubers have raved about how the device is a steal and you should buy it right now—just click the link in bio. [ From our August 2026 issue: The end of reading is here ] And so I did. On Amazon, the X3 is $69 and tops the “hot new releases” list for e-readers, beating out a slew of Kindles. In person, the Xteink is many things: plasticky. Flawed. Finicky. Nevertheless, it is the single best piece of technology that I have purchased in years. In the two months before getting this cartoonishly tiny e-reader, I finished only one book. In one month with the X3, I read three books without even really trying—and my iPhone’s average daily screen time dipped by 25 minutes. The X3 is great because of its size, not in spite of it. (For once, “fun-size” actually lives up to the billing.) Because this is such a runt of a device, you can stick it to your phone and have an e-reader in your pocket at all times. As a result, I’ve found myself reading on my morning commute, in line at a museum, even while waiting through Netflix ads. The display on my Xteink may be roughly half the size of the smallest Kindle, but the text is big enough to easily read. Even after three straight hours of inching through The Power Broker , my eyes weren’t strained. The device’s size actually helped me develop a different relationship to reading altogether: Because each “page” on the Xteink amounts to just a paragraph or two—and sometimes less—I’m compelled to finish it. And now that I’m onto the next page, I might as well finish that one too. A YouTuber who recently reviewed the Xteink had the same experience—she referred to the uniquely addictive experience of using the device as the “Ti
title: This Tiny E-Reader Is the Single Best Piece of Technology in Years

content: O ne simple rule shapes Kansas politics: Republicans win statewide. In U.S. Senate races, the GOP has prevailed without interruption for more than 90 years. But the rule has a corollary, which accounts for the occasional Democratic governor. A Republican thought to be too extreme, too ideological, or too big for their britches can be beaten by a centrist Democrat when the wind blows just right. And so, on the same August Tuesday that saw Michigan Democrats choose Abdul El-Sayed, Kansas Republicans realized their safe seat might not be so safe. Kansas Democrats had picked a man who extols moderation as a matter of faith—literally. Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of America’s largest mainline Protestant congregation, will challenge the first-term incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in November. In the handful of months since he announced his candidacy, Hamilton has defeated 10 garden-variety Democrats in the primary while setting new records for Kansas fundraising, pulling in $1 million in his first week and nearly $3.7 million in his first quarter. Political analysts continue to rate Hamilton a long shot; admittedly, they have nine decades of justification. But Marshall ticks every box that can mean trouble for otherwise-invulnerable Kansas Republicans. Full of himself even by senatorial standards (one Republican Senate colleague described him to me as a “know-it-all”), Marshall is leery of public forums where he might hear from protesters and tends to speak before thinking—a hazard of his appetite for cable-TV appearances. In nearly six years as a constituent of the senator, I have traveled from one end of Kansas to the other, and I have concluded that passionate supporters of Roger Marshall are the electoral equivalent of jackalopes: If they exist, I have never found one. Should Hamilton break the Senate’s longest GOP win streak, he would score more than an enormous off-year upset; his influence on 2028—a free-for-all to define post–Donald Trump politics—could be even larger. Because Hamilton seeks to vindicate the belief, beleaguered in today’s culture, that moderation is a good thing, not just as an electoral strategy, but as an approach to life. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: Texans will decide if Jesus was a lefty ] In Texas, James Talarico’s Christianity seems, at times, to dovetail with uncanny precision with the agenda of secular progressivism. Hamilton’s rhetoric suggests that his Democratic revival tent would be roomier, but at the same time he has so far faced relatively little pressure to translate his disposition into details. He is motivated by “compassion, a belief in safety nets for vulnerable people,” he told me, and also by “fiscal responsibility, limited government, and strong defense.” Such inoffensive straddling may be out of step with today’s politics. “People are really pissing mad, really, really pissing mad,” El-Sayed explained to Michelle Goldberg of The New York Times . content: Wendell Berry was not an easy man to reach. When I wanted to interview him for this magazine in the spring of 2015, his publicist warned me that a press request would take some doing. Berry didn’t have a cellphone. He didn’t use email. He didn’t even have a computer. He wrote most of his drafts by hand during the day, without electric light. And he definitely didn’t make himself available to any old reporter who wanted to talk. I knew this already, of course. Berry, who died on Monday at the age of 92, lived a life defined by acts of radical abstention. He said no emphatically and often; principled refusal was a central theme of his writing and the lore that surrounded him. The publicist spent the better part of a week trying to reach Berry on my behalf. This involved multiple phone calls to his farmhouse, in Henry County, Kentucky, where Berry and his wife, Tanya, had lived since the mid-1960s. Wendell spent most of his time outdoors, the publicist explained, so he often simply wasn’t around to hear the landline ring. After a while, though, she told me that she and Berry had managed to connect, and that he would consider my request. He asked that I write him a letter about the article I had in mind, which I emailed to the publicist so she could print it out and send it to him by post. [ From the February 1991 issue: Out of your car, off your horse ] A few weeks later, I received a voicemail from a number I didn’t recognize. “Hello, Mr. Fassler,” said a voice that was deep and hoarse with age. “This is Wendell Berry.” A giant of Luddism was speaking out of my iPhone. He asked me to call him back. When we spoke, he told me in a warm, genial way that I was out of luck. “I’m just so covered up with work,” he said, “and I can’t tell if it’s because I’m just busy or because I’m old.” But he’d thought a bit about my letter. I’d asked him to take part in “ By Heart ,” a series in which authors discussed the passages from literature that had most shaped their writing and outlook. He said that his forthcoming book, Our Only World , contained a section that the magazine might adapt in some way. It hinged on some verses from Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, as described in the Gospel of Matthew: “Take no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” He asked me to read that section of his book, and to call him back once I had so that we could talk. So I did. And I’ve been thinking about its message ever since. I was surprised, at first, that Berry felt so drawn to this specific moment from the Bible. Jesus’s instruction to not worry about the future seemed at odds with much of what Berry had written. Many of the social and environmental problems that Berry railed against were really problems of short-term thinking, including the pursuit of quick profit, the extractive poisoning of the land, and the love of cheap thrills over deeper, more hard-won pleasures. “Think not of tomorro
title: Why Wendell Berry Didn’t Worry About the Future
author: Joe Fassler

content: When J. D. Vance was asked at a press conference on Thursday about his relationship with Tucker Carlson, the media personality and ultra-right-wing conspiracy theorist, he displayed a surprising side of himself: human, vulnerable, almost touchingly naive. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things,” the vice president said. “And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them. I think that is a terrible place for the United States to go. And if you have a disagreement with somebody politically, even over a deeply held issue, you should still be friends with that person, because the whole republic depends on people of different perspectives being able to talk to one another.” This was a matter not of politics, Vance was at pains to emphasize, but of friendship . If Vance were to renounce Carlson over a matter as trivial as, say, Carlson’s oddly positive assessment of Adolf Hitler, what hope is there for society? The bonds of affection between Vance and Carlson are the very glue holding together the American experiment. And yet, tempting though it might be to imagine Vance clasping hands with the children of the world and teaching them to sing in perfect harmony, some notes of skepticism are warranted. Perhaps Vance’s affection for Carlson has more to do with holding the loyalty of his friend’s enormous audience. [ Peter Wehner: What J. D. Vance once knew ] For one, Vance is not known for cordially disagreeing with people. He has accumulated an unusual number of bitter enemies by flinging insults at people—including Senate Democrats (“You’re full of shit, and everyone knows it”), reporters (“scumbags”), and “childless cat ladies.” Last month, Vance hurled himself into an obscure debate over burrito prices to make a gratuitous swipe at a conservative Washington Post columnist’s weight. At the very same press conference where he waxed so earnestly about open dialogue, Vance mocked the idea that he would talk to former President Biden at the 9/11 ceremony (“I’m really looking forward to hanging out with Joe Biden. I’m sure that we’ll have many, many intense intellectual conversations, and it’ll be great”) and dismissed the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as “a crazy person.” Vance’s dig at El-Sayed, and the context in which he made it, revealed a lot more about his reasons for maintaining the alliance with Carlson than did his encomium to friendship. Vance was trying to illustrate that he and Carlson do not agree on everything. Carlson had recently praised El-Sayed as “America First” and “literally Trumpian,” apparently calculating that the candidate’s anti-Zionism outweighs his many left-wing positions. That view was the one Vance chose to highlight as his point of disagreement, rather than several other controversial remarks Carlson has made. content: Students returning to campus this semester are arriving with a great deal of anxiety about AI and what it will mean for their lives after college. They are right to be worried. New research from Stanford shows that, even though the much-hyped AI job apocalypse has yet to materialize, the technology has already caused a nearly 20 percent drop in employment for young workers in AI-exposed occupations, such as computer programming and customer-service work. Anxiety over the looming threat of AI may seem novel, but as a cognitive scientist who has long studied how fear affects learning and performance, I am all too familiar with this kind of unease. This is how I know it is also curable. Several years ago, my former graduate student Ian Lyons and I invited people who were anxious about math to have their brains scanned while they took a math test. We were surprised to find that it wasn’t the test itself that sent people’s brains into a panic. Rather, the neural signals associated with threat detection and pain were most acute when people were merely anticipating the test. [ John Paul Rollert: A society of cheats ] We are all now living through AI’s waiting-for-the-math-test phase. AI is transforming classrooms, workplaces, and hiring needs—and experts say more turbulence is coming. Teachers and students are struggling to parse the difference between deploying AI effectively and exploiting the technology to cheat. But rather than tackling this disruptive change and the resulting anxiety head-on, many educators are trying to make AI simply go away. The University of Chicago’s social-science faculty have prohibited most technology and banned the use of AI tools from their core classes. Although law firms are beginning to embrace the benefits of generative AI, the technology apparently makes many law schools squeamish. In May, the UC Berkeley School of Law announced that students are prohibited from using AI in “conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit.” The University of Chicago Law School has decided to ban all screens from first-year classrooms entirely. In an atmosphere of uncertainty—and given prevailing concerns about students using AI to cheat—such bans would seem to make some sense. But draconian mandates and screenless classes can’t be the only ways that colleges deal with AI. If universities hope to remain relevant in a world shaped by artificial intelligence, they should strive to guide students to understand and use these tools productively. In my research of math anxiety, we found that the best cure was practicing math. This points to a way forward. When we supply students with the space to thoughtfully explore and engage with these tools, we can help ensure that they graduate into an AI-enabled workforce with more confidence and competence than fear, and with an appreciation for how to use AI tools ethically. content: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. The crypto industry has always moved in cycles: booms and busts; bull markets and harsh, unforgiving “winters.” We’re in something of a lull right now: Bitcoin, the original cryptocurrency, is worth about two-thirds of what it was last fall. Meanwhile, investors are turning their attention to flashier innovations in artificial intelligence. About half of Americans now use AI chatbots, whereas just about a fifth of the country has ever used or invested in crypto. But the crypto industry isn’t dead—as of today, the combined value of all digital currencies is still more than $2.7 trillion—and neither are its political ambitions. Crypto companies have so far put $206 million toward this year’s midterm elections, more than any other corporate sector, including the AI industry, according to a Public Citizen analysis of OpenSecrets and Federal Election Commission data. Fairshake, the industry’s foremost super PAC, has a giant war chest and a reputation for backing winners from both parties (Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has reportedly warned of the risks of crossing it). Crypto is much further from the spotlight now than it was during its 2024 election-spending spree; back then, the industry was flush with cash, but its reputation was still recovering from the crash of two years prior and from the spectacle of Sam Bankman-Fried’s fraud trial. Even as Americans continue to distrust crypto, they’re now reserving their outrage for other corners of the tech industry, such as data centers and surveillance cameras. Although crypto is no longer as central to the public conversation, it’s still finding ways to flex its power. Fairshake first established itself as a major force during the 2024 election cycle, spending about $133 million in support of its chosen candidates. It started 2026 with a reported $193 million in the bank and has so far spent close to $70 million elevating politicians with an industry-friendly agenda. Fairshake’s record this year has been incredibly strong . Despite a few fairly significant losses , 50 of the 54 candidates it backed ended up winning their race. Not all of them won entirely because of Fairshake’s intervention: Some were incumbents who didn’t have a serious challenger. The group spent more than $12 million to get a pro-crypto Republican into the general election for Alabama’s open Senate seat—it was “by far the biggest spender” in the primary, per The New York Times . content: When did AI companies become AI labs ? That term, and the image of studious, exacting white-coated scientists that it conjures, has become curiously entrenched as a descriptor for the businesses swiftly escorting the world into an existentially unsettling future. AI companies themselves have embraced the label: When Chris Olah, a co-founder of Anthropic, addressed the pope earlier this year, he repeatedly referred to his company, one of the most powerful AI enterprises in the world, as a lab. Industry press releases, technology commentators, and news publications have all picked up the word too. You’ll see the term on transit advertisements in San Francisco and in the pages of The New York Times (and, yes, The Atlantic ). Here is my proposal: Everyone, please stop. This term has gone too far. Although AI companies do invest heavily in research and development, using a word typically associated with groups of truth-seeking scientists is misleading, odd, and too favorable to these companies’ own ends. As a software engineer working in tech, I’ve seen little evidence that AI companies’ research practices differ significantly from those of the rest of the tech industry. Google and Microsoft, for example, have robust research divisions, but we still call them companies. So why has the laboratory term become so deeply enmeshed with AI? Part of the reason is historical. Over the past century, research laboratories have played a crucial role in computer science. Studies performed at Bell Labs, one of America’s first industrial labs, resulted in the development of the transistor and the cellular network. In the 1970s, scientists at the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science pioneered the foundations of modern cryptography. As the Harvard historian Steven Shapin writes in his book The Scientific Life , countless innovations such as these that originated in corporate labs during the 20th century helped change the public’s perception of science. No longer simply knowledge for knowledge’s sake, science became viewed as a key engine of societal and economic progress. In their early years, OpenAI and Anthropic mainly performed research, similar to other industrial labs. Since then, however, they have commercialized rapidly: Each company is now valued near $1 trillion and generates billions in quarterly revenue. Holding on to the lab label seems to have the obvious PR benefit of allowing both companies to lean into their scientific legacy. Because of concerns about child safety, privacy, and job displacement, Americans largely hold a negative perception of the industry—and tech as a whole. That’s translated into popular opposition from politicians, data-center activists, and religious leaders who are concerned about the outsize influence of these companies: Spending on AI as a share of U.S. GDP now rivals defense spending . Meanwhile, scientists remain relatively popular. A 2026 Pew Research Center poll found that more than 75 percent of Americans trust scientists
title: There’s No Such Thing as an AI ‘Lab’
author: Matthew Sun

content: During the five weeks of her murder trial, Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three young children in 2023, spoke barely a word. She has been on display for the entirety of her livestreamed trial, sitting in her wheelchair beside her lawyer at the defense table. At one point, when the prosecution walked the jury through the children’s autopsy reports, she hunched over, racked with sobs, crying out, “I can’t do this!” But mostly, Clancy has remained silent and wide-eyed, her gaze wandering around the courtroom as though searching for something. The judge in the case has just declared a mistrial because the jury has been unable to reach a unanimous verdict. But the viewing public, in the absence of Clancy’s own explanation of her experiences leading up to and after the killings, has projected its own ideas onto the case and rendered its own verdict. Some people have interpreted Clancy’s trial as a referendum on women’s postpartum mental health. Others have developed elaborate conspiracy theories maintaining that Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick, is actually the guilty party. Still others have construed Clancy’s story as evidence for their own niche political beliefs. These are all comforting narratives, in some sense, because they imply an underlying logic that imbues the events with meaning and provides a road map for catharsis. Yet the jury’s inability to arrive at a verdict makes plain that a careful evaluation of the facts does not yield an easily intelligible conclusion. The reality may be darker and more despairing: that something so dramatic and destructive could, in the end, mean nothing at all. As Clancy’s trial has progressed, dozens of women wearing pink have appeared at organized rallies outside the courthouse in Plymouth, Massachusetts, holding signs signaling a kind of support for her. “Any one of us who have dealt with mental health, anxiety, depression, postpartum—I think we just know that any one of us could be sitting in her chair,” the organizer of a recent event billed as an opportunity to “stand in peace for Lindsay” told a local news outlet. There is something inherently unsettling about any public expression of support for a confessed killer, but these gatherings and their associated social-media movements have not seemed aimed at improving Clancy’s odds of success in court. Instead, these demonstrations suggest that Clancy has for some women become a symbolic figure : the devoted but suffering mother martyred by the relentless, punishing demands of her children’s early years and left to suffer by a flawed and fractured health-care system. Many women have felt overwhelmed to the point of drowning in the months after giving birth, and many have sought help but failed to receive it. Clancy’s case, in her supporters’ imagination, appears to be the sum of all those biological and social hazards. What happened to Clancy, in this view, was predictable, and thus preventable. content: Jon Ronson had never really thought about the term masculinity until a strange series of events led him down a rabbit hole involving castles, cage fights, and an actor playing a horse. Host Charlie Warzel talks to Ronson about the disinhibited men who are looking for purpose in all the wrong places. Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube The following is a transcript of the episode: Jon Ronson: So I think, beginning with deindustrialization, the death of factories, office life eroding, men realizing that certain privileges they had they don’t quite have the same way anymore—feeling kind of tossed around in a sea of conflicting ideologies about what being a man actually means. Should you be more stoical? Should you be more vulnerable? You know, all of these men’s-health influencers giving these differing, contrasting ideas. And so this is a huge societal shift in many different ways. And I think that’s what’s happening. You’ve got men responding to these changes by bowing out, and then you’ve got these other men who are responding by spiraling. Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , and today we are headed down a rabbit hole that includes ominous castles, public shaming, YouTube, White House cage fighting, all to answer one of life’s burning questions. Why is it that so many men are unraveling these days? Is this part of a changing economy? Part of a bad job market? Is it fallout from the pandemic? Or, is it part of something bigger? A societal failure of some sort, or an outgrowth of what some people have called the masculinity crisis? Now those words, masculinity crisis , can cause some people to roll their eyes. Men, of course, continue to enjoy all kinds of societal privilege, and gender inequities abound. But what is clear, I think, if you spent any time engaging with modern politics and culture, is that over the last few decades there has been a very real, if hard to define, debate over what it means to be a man. Jobs and gender roles—they’ve changed, and culture along with it. Much of it for the better. But that change has also created some uncertainty for the men who have been used to being at the center of every household, every office, every institution, marketing campaign, and political decision. And it’s in that uncertainty that all kinds of voices, pickup artists, politicians, incels on 4chan, Andrew Tate, Jordan Peterson—you name it—they’ve all jumped in to offer these competing visions of masculinity. Now, some of this has taken the form of toxic, misogynistic, manosphere bullshit. Some of it is just positive or harmless—“dudes rock” kind of stuff. And so many of these lessons, they end up being taught or absorbed, for better or for worse, in online communities and communicated by people who may or may not have ulterior motives. author: Charlie Warzel

content: Amid soaring measles cases, the U.S. health secretary and leadership at his CDC have picked a fight with the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania about what counts as a measles death. The last thing public health needs is drama when the focus needs to be on responding to the outbreak itself. States have a standard process for notifying the CDC about notifiable diseases , using established case definitions . Developing those definitions is usually a long, deliberative process involving epidemiologists, scientists, and agency review through the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists and the CDC. Right now, that standard process is under threat and will further drive a wedge between states and how they work with the CDC and the administration. Read the rest…
title: Opinion: Make infectious disease data boring again

content: The U.S. retirement landscape has changed dramatically in recent decades. As traditional defined benefit (DB) pensions have declined , workers have become increasingly reliant on employer-sponsored defined contribution (DC) plans such as 401(k)s to finance their retirement. In 2025, approximately 80 million American households had a participant in a DC plan . Legislation has paved the way for innovations such as automatic enrollment and retirement income features . As Americans continue to shoulder greater responsibility for their own retirement security, however, many still face the prospect of inadequate savings . Policymakers and industry leaders are exploring additional strategies to improve long-term outcomes, including changing the investment options available in DC plans. Background In August 2025, President Trump issued an executive order outlining plans to “democratize access” to alternative assets in workplace retirement accounts. Alternative assets are a broad category, including private equity, private credit, real estate, and digital assets held through professionally managed funds, among others—investments that are distinct from the publicly traded stocks and bonds that make up the overwhelming majority of 401(k) assets. The order instructed the Department of Labor (DOL) to clarify how fiduciaries should evaluate these assets, sparking policy discussion about their place in retirement plans. On March 31, 2026, DOL published a proposed rule addressing how DC plan fiduciaries satisfy their duty of prudence under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) when selecting any designated investment alternative—the investment options that a plan fiduciary chooses to make available on the participant menu. The proposal outlines a non-exhaustive list of six factors—performance, fees, liquidity, valuation, benchmarking, and complexity. It pairs that list with a process-based safe harbor under which a fiduciary who “objectively, thoroughly, and analytically” considers and reaches a determination on any of the six factors is presumed to have acted prudently as to that factor. The rule aims to ease the inclusion of alternative assets in retirement plans and mitigate litigation risk . The executive order directed DOL to focus on target date funds and other funds that hold a mix of investments, but the department issued a broader rule that reaches any investment option on a plan menu, meaning private assets could be offered on their own rather than only within a diversified fund. The comment period closed on June 1, 2026, and the rule has not been finalized. Although DOL’s proposed rule addresses all asset classes, this article focuses on private equity and private credit, whose broad adoption in the DB space makes them a consequential test case for the factors DOL has asked fiduciaries to weigh. content: The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) released its latest Point-in-Time (PIT) count , finding that 745,652 people experienced homelessness on a single night in January of 2025. This figure is the first year-over-year decline since 2016 and roughly 3% lower than the 2024 count (771,480)—the highest number on record since HUD standardized its PIT count methodology in 2007. Beneath this top-line number, the national picture on homelessness is more complicated: individual and chronic homelessness hit record highs in 2025, homelessness among those 65 and older continued to rise, and 28 states saw an overall increase in homelessness. The net national year-over-year decrease was largely driven by trends in just two states. This blog answers key questions about the 2025 PIT count. What Drove the Overall Decline in Homelessness? The decrease in homelessness in 2025 is largely attributable to trends in New York and Illinois, where 23,800 fewer people experienced homelessness than in 2024. The reduction in these two states alone accounts for more than 90% of the gross national decrease reflected in the 2025 PIT count. New York and Illinois experienced large increases in homelessness in 2024, likely related to an influx of asylum seekers straining shelter systems in New York City and Chicago. The 2025 decline in homelessness in these two states is best understood as progress toward reversing the 2024 spike. This progress has been incremental and uneven: Illinois reversed roughly 80% of its 2024 influx, while New York has walked back less than 25% of its surge. Homelessness is also rising outside of major cities: suburban Continuums of Care (CoCs) saw a roughly 2% increase in homelessness and 28 states reported higher overall counts than in 2024. How Have Chronic and Individual Homelessness Changed? Chronic homelessness , defined as prolonged or repeated periods of homelessness with a co-occurring disabling condition, rose to a record-high 155,750 people in 2025, a 2% increase from 2024 and a nearly 90% increase since 2015 . One in three homeless individuals is now chronically homeless. While the number of permanent supportive housing beds for chronically homeless individuals rose by 8% in 2025, demand continues to outpace capacity.  Unsheltered chronic homelessness declined by 3%, the first such decrease since 2018 , suggesting that outreach and encampment resolution efforts are beginning to move some of the most entrenched cases indoors. The number of homeless individuals—those not in families—reached a record high of 515,286 in 2025. This group comprises more than 90% of those experiencing chronic homelessness. How Has Family Homelessness Changed? The 2025 PIT count is encouraging with respect to homelessness among families with children, showing an 11% decrease.
